3.text: reindeer-sledge, and a peculiar kind of harness (Fig. 20, b), identical with that

4.text: used by the American Eskimo. They harnessed the dogs abreast in the same

5.text: way as is done in North America. Since that time, however, they have entirely

6.text: abandoned the old mode of dog-driving, and have adopted the southern form

7.text: of sledge and the “tandem” method of attachment. Nelson¹ gives a sketch

8.text: of a dog-sledge from Plover Bay, on the Siberian Pacific coast, which seems

9.text: to me rather to be a reindeer-sledge, as it is too long and slender to be

10.text: driven with dogs. It is somewhat strange that he did not see any other dog-

11.text: sledge on the Siberian shore. Nordenskiöld,² too, gives a sketch of a dog-

12.text: sledge similar to a reindeer pack-sledge. Of the native drawings reproduced

13.text: in his book, one represents a man driving a similar sledge with three dogs

14.text: harnessed abreast and a leader ahead; and another pictures a man driving

15.text: an ordinary East Siberian dog-sledge with a tandem team. Lieut. Nordquist,

16.text: in his Report given by Nordenskiöld,³ describes likewise the old method of

17.text: dog-harnessing; but Nordenskiöld says elsewhere that it was used only for

18.text: short trips, and that almost all drivers that passed along the coast on a

19.text: prolonged journey had dogs attached tandem fashion. The old method of

20.text: harnessing has gone entirely out of use; and I have never seen it employed

21.text: in Maritime villages, though poor Reindeer people along the seacoast, when

22.text: using dogs, sometimes attach them to a reindeer-sledge. Among the Asiatic

23.text: Eskimo there are cases (for example, in the ceremonial races in the spring)

24.text: in which the dogs are still attached in the old way (Plate VII, Fig. 1).

25.text: A model made in Mariinsky Post shows that the bone eyes at the ends

26.text: of the long traces were strung on a line tied across the sledge in front of

27.text: the first cross-piece joining the rails. This line is more or less similar to that

28.text: of the Eskimo sledge described by Boas.⁴

30.text: were attached singly to small sledges by means of a wooden shaft, or even

31.text: with a small wooden yoke, in a manner similar to that used for harnessing
